title: About

Background

I went Colby College for my undergraduate degree, double majoring in Data and Environmental Science. During that time I spent a semester at the Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences. My interest in urban spatial analytics stems from the summer research I conducted with the 7 Lakes Alliance. I performed a geochemical and spatial analysis of the sediment in North Pond, identifying the main source of iron influx which was causing algal blooms. I created a heat map to communicate this and presented to the local community. Without many geospatial classes (all but 2) at Colby, I wanted more experience with geospatial analysis, which has led me here to UPenn. I hope to help solve environmental problems and contribute to urban planning projects in Bangkok, my home town, to build a more sustainable and accesible city.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
** Maine is one of the least populated states and is the most forested in the entire country, which means people are spread apart with long distances to travel. In this analysis, I look at the travel time to work across counties in Maine, and test the reliability of the data between each area.**

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Choosing what to measure

my_state <- params$state
my_variable <- "B08303_001" # total travel time to work

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,

)

Let’s look at what came back.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Most margins of error are in the 1.5-4.75% range relative to the estimate.
Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                      estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                        <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Piscataquis County, Maine     6606   314    4.75
 2 Franklin County, Maine       12103   543    4.49
 3 Sagadahoc County, Maine      16024   661    4.13
 4 Lincoln County, Maine        14665   535    3.65
 5 Waldo County, Maine          15616   542    3.47
 6 Knox County, Maine           16077   540    3.36
 7 Washington County, Maine     11149   360    3.23
 8 Oxford County, Maine         23238   742    3.19
 9 Somerset County, Maine       19930   603    3.03
10 Hancock County, Maine        23866   701    2.94


Piscataquis County, which is in central-northern Maine has the highest margin of error percentage at 4.75% of the estimate.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

# observe spread of MOE percentage valuess
hist(county_data$moe_pct)









county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 2.5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 3.5 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence     4
2 Low confidence      4
3 Moderate            8


For these counties, the margin of error percentage was relatively low, which meant using the 5% and 10% cutoffs for high and moderate confidence were unsuitable. Instead, a 2.5% cutoff was used for high confidence and 3.5% was used for moderate confidence instead. 4 counties had high and low confidence, while 8 had moderate confidence.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                       myvarE myvarM   popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                       <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 23001 Androscoggin County, Maine  48226   1013 112323    NA
2 23003 Aroostook County, Maine     26005    704  67227    NA
3 23005 Cumberland County, Maine   134152   2045 305940    NA
4 23007 Franklin County, Maine      12103    543  30145    NA
5 23009 Hancock County, Maine       23866    701  56084    NA
6 23011 Kennebec County, Maine      51512   1295 125614    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 2.5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 3.5 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence          4        196641.
2 Low confidence           4         30051.
3 Moderate                 8         58829 


The average population for high confidence counties were many times higher than other confidence categories. Counties with low confidence had the lowest average population by far. Based on these results, higher populations may produce more representative data, as outliers are better dealt with in larger sample sizes.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy



Maine Counties and Cities Map


The following counties had the highest margin of error (in order): Piscataquis, Franklin, Sagadahoc, and Lincoln county. These counties had some of the lowest populations in the entire state. Generally, smaller sample sizes yield more frequent outliers and a normal distribution is less expected due to the lack of “average” samples. Counties with the highest confidence were the most populous. These counties included Cumberland, Androscoggin, Penobscot, and York. York and Cumberland are the most southern counties, which make them that much closer to the rest of New England. Cumberland is also home to the better Portland and Bowdoin College. Interestingly, counties that had colleges outside of Portland, such as Bates, UMaine, or Colby, had higher confidences. With the presence of these colleges, population counting is more accurate. Ignoring margins of error can be harmful, especially when the data may not be representative of the target population. In this case, the time spent traveling in a low reliability county may not actually be accurate. Hypothetically, if this county actually had a much higher travel time to work compared to what the data says, they may not get the appropriate allocation of funding for infrastructure and road development. This can be harmful when the data says another county has high travel time, despite that not being true, which can lead to funding cuts for a county that actually needs it.

Write Function and Iterate
Does the small-places-are-noisier pattern hold everywhere, or are some states different?

data_pull <- function(variable, state) {
  get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
  ) %>%
    mutate(state = state)
}

states <- c("AZ", "HI", "TX", "AK", "WY", "SC", "NJ")
var <- "B08303_001"

multi_state_data <- map_dfr(states, ~data_pull(variable = var, state = .x)) %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  )) %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct))

multi_state_data %>%
  group_by(state, reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  ) %>%
  arrange(state, reliability)

The principle still holds where smaller populations have lower reliability.


Change the geographic scale

my_variable <- "B08303_001"

knox_tract_data <- get_acs(

title: Week 3: ggplot & errors
text:
Key Concepts

Coefficient of variation (CV)

Relative measure of sampling error
Low CV < 15% –> high reliability
Medium CV = 15-30% –> moderate reliability
High CV > 30% –> low reliability



Measures of Uncertainty

Standard error (SE): MOE / 1.645
Derived uncertainty: margins of error of numerator and denominator can’t be simply computed

moe_sum -> adding estimates together
moe_prop -> one estimate as share of another
moe_ratio -> one not a subset of another




Change Over Time

Compare non-overlapping intervals: calculate change between intervals and uncertainty of both estimates
SE_diff: sqrt(SE1^2 + SE2^2)
CI of Change: Difference +- (1.645 * SE_diff)
CV = (SE / Estimate) x 100
z = change / SE_diff
significant = abs(z) > 1.645
Compare overlapping intervals:

I assumed some of the time period for some of the claims: Fairhill, Holmesburg, Tioga-Nicetown and the income gap. No years were specified for these so I assumed 2013-2017 based on the title. The time periods that overlap are 2013-2017 and 2016-2017. However, the 1-year ACS data is not available at the tract level due to the area 65,000 population requirement. The Census Bureau does not recommend comparing different time-period lengths as they measure characteristics of the population in different ways.

Assignment 3: Verify the Claim of Povery Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 2: Test

Calculate Poverty Rate


Show code
grouped_neighborhoods_2006 <- grouped_neighborhoods_2006 %>%
  mutate(pov_rate = (total_poverty / total_pop) * 100,
         pov_rate_moe = moe_prop(total_poverty, total_pop, total_poverty_moe, total_pop_moe),
         pov_moe_pct = (pov_rate_moe / pov_rate) * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
  pov_moe_pct < 12  ~ "High",
  pov_moe_pct < 40 ~ "Moderate",
  TRUE         ~ "Low"
  ))
  
grouped_neighborhoods_2013 <- grouped_neighborhoods_2013 %>%
  mutate(pov_rate = (total_poverty / total_pop) * 100,
         pov_rate_moe = moe_prop(total_poverty, total_pop, total_poverty_moe, total_pop_moe),
         pov_moe_pct = (pov_rate_moe / pov_rate) * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
  pov_moe_pct < 12  ~ "High",
  pov_moe_pct < 40 ~ "Moderate",
  TRUE         ~ "Low"
  ))




View Reliability of Each Neighborhood as a Data Table


Show code
library(gt)

reliability_table <- grouped_neighborhoods_2006 %>%
  mutate(
    dot = case_when(
      pov_moe_pct < 12  ~ "🟢",
      pov_moe_pct <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE              ~ "🔴"
    ),
    flag = case_when(
      pov_moe_pct < 12  ~ "Reliable",
      pov_moe_pct <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE              ~ "Unreliable"
    ),
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(pov_moe_pct)) %>%
  select(dot, LISTNAME, pov_rate, pov_rate_moe, pov_moe_pct, flag)

reliability_table %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(pov_rate, pov_rate_moe), decimals = 0) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = pov_moe_pct, decimals = 1) %>%
  cols_label(
    dot               = "",
    LISTNAME          = "Neighborhood",
    pov_rate          = "Poverty Rate",
    pov_rate_moe      = "MOE",
    pov_moe_pct       = "CV (%)",
    flag              = "Reliability"
  ) %>%
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = dot) %>%

Reliability thresholds follow Jurjevich et al. (2018): CV < 12% reliable, 12–40% somewhat reliable, > 40% unreliable.










Calculate change between two time periods and margin of error of this change


Show code
selected_2006 <- select(grouped_neighborhoods_2006, 
                        c(LISTNAME, pov_rate_2006 = pov_rate, pov_moe_2006 = pov_rate_moe,
                          median_income_2006 = median_income, income_moe_2006 = median_income_moe))
selected_2013 <- select(grouped_neighborhoods_2013,
                        c(LISTNAME, pov_rate_2013 = pov_rate, pov_moe_2013 = pov_rate_moe,
                          median_income_2013 = median_income, income_moe_2013 = median_income_moe))

comparison_df <- inner_join(selected_2006,selected_2013, by = "LISTNAME") %>%
  na.omit(comparison_df)

pov_comparison <- comparison_df %>%
  mutate(
    pov_change = pov_rate_2013 - pov_rate_2006,
    se_1     = pov_moe_2013 / 1.645,
    se_2     = pov_moe_2006 / 1.645,
    se_diff  = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z        = pov_change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  )

income_comparison <- comparison_df %>%
  mutate(
    income_change = median_income_2013 - median_income_2006,
    se_1     = income_moe_2013 / 1.645,
    se_2     = income_moe_2006 / 1.645,
    se_diff  = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z        = income_change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  )

pov_comparison %>%
  count(significant)

  significant     n
  <lgl>       <int>
1 TRUE          158




View Biggest Percent Changes


Show code
pov_comparison %>%
  filter(significant) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(LISTNAME, pov_change), y = pov_change)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = pov_change > 0)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = pov_change - moe_diff,
                    ymax = pov_change + moe_diff), width = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Statistically significant change in poverty count",
       subtitle = "2006–2010 vs 2013–2017, ACS 5-year estimates",
       x = "Neighborhoods", y = "Change in people below poverty level (%)")









All neighborhoods that had data were highly reliable. The only unreliable neighborhood was the airport, which didn’t have any data in the first place. Out of the 159 neighborhoods, all 159 had statistically significant changes to their poverty rate. East Park, Navy Yard, Brewerytown, and Packer Park experienced the biggest decrease in poverty rate, while Penrose and Chinatown saw the greatest rise in poverty rate.
The only neighborhood that produce NAs was the airport, because its population and poverty columns were 0 due to no one living there. Division with 0 will produce NAs as it is not possible. Because it was the only neighborhood that had an NA, I removed it from the comparison data frame. If there had been more neighborhoods with NAs, I would explore ACS data sets from other years to find more complete data.

Claims that are supported

The poverty rate in Eastwick did indeed increased from 12% to 26% between the 2006-2010 and 2013-2017 ACS. The high reliability also indicates this statistic is trustworthy.

Claims that are unsupported

Fairhill did not have a 61% poverty rate in either ACS data sets, as the poverty rate hovered around 55%. The Holmesburg claim is completely wrong. The poverty rate was never 2% and never reach the 19% as the article suggests. Its poverty rate was 14% in 2006-2010 and increased significantly to ~18% in 2013-2017. Lastly, the median income of Nicetown decreased significantly, but did not match the figures the article suggested. In 2006-2010, the median household income of Nicetown was 99,815, decreasing to 72,443 by the time of the next 5-year ACS. Tioga had a median household income of 307,688 in 2006-2010, declining to 296,165 by 2013-2017, which was an insignificant decrease.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim of Povery Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 4: Rewrite
Between the 2006-2010 and 2013-2017 ACS data sets, the Eastwick neighborhood experienced a poverty rate increase from 12% to 26%, which was statistically significant. Holemesburg saw a 4% increase in its poverty rate, which was significant in the neighborhood’s context. Fairhill had a high, but consistent poverty rate of 55% across the two ACS time spans. Lastly, both Tioga and Nicetown experienced a decrease in median income: 307,688 to 296,165 for the former and 99,815 to 72,443 for the latter. Due to the high median income in Tioga, this was not a significant change. However, the decrease in income was significant for Nicetown.
